name: Video Quality Drift
description: Measures quality metric drift over video duration — AI-generated video may show systematic quality degradation patterns.
mechanism:
This method detects AI-generated video by analyzing how video quality metrics evolve over the duration of the clip — AI generators produce characteristic quality drift patterns absent in authentic footage:

1. **Multi-Metric Quality Profiling**: The method computes multiple no-reference quality metrics for each frame to build a temporal quality profile: (a) BRISQUE (Blind/Referenceless Image Spatial Quality Evaluator) — measures naturalness of image statistics using MSCN (mean-subtracted contrast-normalized) coefficients; authentic video shows BRISQUE scores of 20–40 while AI-generated often exceeds 45, (b) NIQE (Natural Image Quality Evaluator) — compares image statistics to a pre-learned model of pristine natural images, (c) sharpness — measured as the average gradient magnitude, (d) noise level — estimated from the finest wavelet scale, (e) structural complexity — measured as JPEG compressed file size normalized by pixel count. These five metrics are computed for every frame, producing five time series that capture quality evolution.

2. **Temporal Quality Stability Analysis**: Authentic video captured by a single camera in a single shot should exhibit stable quality metrics — BRISQUE, NIQE, sharpness, and noise level should not change significantly unless there is a physical reason (focus change, exposure change, motion). The method analyzes: (a) quality variance — the temporal standard deviation of each metric within a shot should be small (CV < 0.05 for authentic), (b) quality trend — authentic video may show slight trends from auto-exposure adjustments, but these are monotonic and slow; AI-generated video may show oscillating quality or sudden jumps, (c) quality autocorrelation — authentic quality metrics have high temporal autocorrelation (lag-1 > 0.95 within a shot) because physical conditions change slowly; AI-generated video may show lower autocorrelation (< 0.85) due to per-frame quality variations.

3. **Autoregressive Quality Degradation**: Many AI video generators use autoregressive or sliding-window approaches that produce a characteristic quality degradation pattern: (a) the first few frames (within the initial context window) show highest quality, (b) quality gradually degrades as the generator accumulates errors over longer sequences — visible as increasing BRISQUE scores and decreasing sharpness over time, (c) periodic quality 'resets' may occur at chunk boundaries where the generator re-initializes. The method fits a linear regression to the quality time series and checks: authentic video has near-zero slope (|slope| < 0.1 BRISQUE points/second), while AI-generated video may show slopes of 0.5–2.0 points/second. The method also checks for periodic quality modulation by computing the autocorrelation of the quality derivative.

4. **Cross-Metric Quality Coherence**: In physically captured video, different quality metrics should be correlated — when sharpness decreases (e.g., defocus), noise in the blurred region also decreases, NIQE increases, and structural complexity drops. The method computes the pairwise correlation matrix of the five quality metrics across time and validates that correlations match physical expectations: (a) sharpness and structural complexity should be positively correlated (r > 0.7), (b) noise and BRISQUE should be positively correlated (r > 0.5), (c) sharpness and NIQE should be negatively correlated (r < -0.3). AI-generated video often shows decorrelated quality metrics — high sharpness with high NIQE, or low noise with high BRISQUE — because the generator's quality variations don't follow physical camera models.
parameters:
Quality metrics: BRISQUE, NIQE, sharpness, noise level, JPEG complexity
BRISQUE range: 20–40 (authentic)
Quality CV threshold: < 0.05 (within shot)
Lag-1 autocorrelation: > 0.95 (authentic)
Quality slope: |slope| < 0.1 points/sec (authentic)
AR degradation: 0.5–2.0 points/sec (AI signature)
Sharpness-complexity correlation: r > 0.7
Noise-BRISQUE correlation: r > 0.5
Minimum video length: 3 seconds
Shot boundary detection: histogram difference
accuracy: 79–87% accuracy detecting AI-generated video via quality drift analysis. Temporal quality stability achieves AUC of 0.85. Autoregressive degradation detection provides F1-score of 0.83. Cross-metric coherence adds 4–6% improvement. Performance increases with video length — longer sequences show more pronounced quality drift. Short clips (< 3 seconds) provide insufficient temporal data.
source: Mittal, A. et al. (2012). No-Reference Image Quality Assessment in the Spatial Domain. IEEE TIP, 21(12), 4695–4708.
useCase: Detecting AI-generated video through quality temporal evolution patterns. Identifying autoregressive generation artifacts in long-form video. Forensic analysis of video editing and concatenation. Quality assurance for video authentication pipelines.
strengths:
• No-reference metrics require no authentic reference video for comparison
• Quality drift is intrinsic to autoregressive generation architectures
• Cross-metric coherence provides physics-based validation
• Works for general video content without scene-specific assumptions
• Complementary to pixel-level and frequency-domain methods
limitations:
• Short video clips provide insufficient temporal data for drift analysis
• High-quality AI generators with temporal attention show less quality drift
• Intentional quality effects (film grain, vignetting) alter baseline metrics
• Live-streamed video may have genuine quality fluctuations from encoding
• Scene changes within the video require shot segmentation before analysis
